text:
5/30/2017  
1 Algorithm  
An algorithm is a finite set of 
instructions that accomplishes a 
particular task  
Properties of an Algorithm  
•Input : Zero  or more  quantities  are supplied  
externally . 
•Output : Atleast  one quantity  is produced . 
•Definiteness : Each  instruction  is clear  and 
unambiguous  
•Finiteness : For all cases,  algorithm  terminates  
after  a finite  number  of steps  
•Effectiveness : Each  instruction  must  be very  
basic . 
5/30/2017  
2 •Algorithms  that are definite  and effective  are also called  
computational  procedures . 
•A program  is the expression  of an algorithm  in a 
programming  language . 
•Active areas in study of algorithms:  
–How  to devise  algorithms : Certain  design  techniques  are 
available . 
–How  to validate  algorithms : To show  that algorithm  produces  
correct  answer  for all possible  legal  inputs  independently  of the 
issues  concerning  programming  language . Once  an algorithm  is 
validated,  program  is written  and verified . 
–How  to analyze  algorithms : Determining  how  much  computing  
time  and storage  an algorithm  requires . Helps  in  making  
quantitative  judgments  about  one algorithm  over  the other . 
Helps  in predicting  whether  software  will meet  efficiency  
constraints?  
–How  to test a program : Two phases : debugging  and profiling  
(performance  measurement)  
Algorithm Specification  
•Algorithm  specification  using  pseudo  code  that resembles  
C. 
–Comments  begin  with  // 
–Block  is represented  by braces  { } 
–Identifier  begins  with  a letter . Simple  data  types  are assumed . 
Compound  data  types  can be formed  using  record . 
  node  = record  
   { datatype_ 1 data 1; 
      … 
      datatype_n  datan ; 
      node*  link; 
   } 
     . And -> can be used  to denote  the fields  of type  node . 
–Assignment  := operator  is used  to assign  values . 
–Two boolean  values  are assumed  true  and false . Logical  and 
relative  operators  are provided . 
5/30/2017  
3 –Multidimensional  array  is accessed  as A[i,j] 
–Looping  constructs  for, while  and repeat  until  are provided . 
•for i:= 1 to 10 step  1 do {…..} 
•while  i<10 do { … } 
•Repeat  {…..} until  (i>10) 
–Break  statement  results  in exit from  innermost  loop .  
–Return  statement  results  in exit of the function . 
–Conditional  statements  if and case  are provided . 
•if (a>b)  then  c:=a else c:=b 
•case   
 { :a=1:  c:=10; 
   :a=2:  c:=20; 
   :else: c:=100; 
 } 
–Input  and output  is performed  using  read  and write  statements  
respectively . 
–Only  one type  of procedure  ‘Algorithm’  is provided  having  a 
heading  and a body . 
–Simple  variables  are passed  by value . Arrays  are passed  by 
reference . 
 
–Example : Selection  sort algorithm . 
•for i:=1 to n do 
        { 
           Examine  a[i] to a[n] and suppose  the smallest  element  is at a[j]; 
            Interchange  a[i] and a[j]; 
        } 
•Example: Selection sort pseudo code program  
1 Algorithm SelectionSort  (a,n) 
 2   // sort the array a[1:n] into increasing order.  
 3   { 
 4      for i:=1 to n do  
 5       {  
 6          j:= i; 
 7          for k:= i+1 to n do  
 8              if (a[k]<a[j]) then j:=k;  
 9          t:=a[ i]; a[i]:=a[j]; a[j]:=t;  
 10     }  
 11  }  
 
5/30/2017  
4 •Recursive Algorithms:  
–A function  that is defined  in terms  of itself  is called  
recursive  function . 
–An algorithm  can be direct  recursive  or indirect  
recursive . 
–Any algorithm  that can be written  using  assignment,  
if-then -else and while  statement  can also be written  
using  assignment,  if-then -else and recursion . 
Sometimes  given  problem  is itself  recursively  defined . 
–Example : Towers  of Hanoi :  
•Three  diamond  towers  are there  out of which  one diamond  
tower  has 64 golden  disks  arranged  in decreasing  size from  
bottom  to top. Disks  are required  to move  from  one tower  
to another  using  the third  tower . Only  one disk can be 
moved  at a time  and at no time  can a disk be on top of a 
smaller  disk. 
–Towers of Hanoi using recursion:  
1Algorithm TowersOfHanoi (n,x,y,z ) 
2{ 
3   if (n>=1) then  
4   { 
5      TowersOfHanoi (n-1,x,z,y);  
6 write (“move top disk from tower”, x, “to top of 
tower”, y);  
7        TowersOfHanoi (n-1,z,y,x)  
8     } 
9  } 
 
     
5/30/2017  
5 •Another example: Permutation Generator:  
–Given a set of n>=1 elements, problem is to print all 
possible permutations. If set is {a, b, c} then set of 
permutations is {( a,b,c ), (a,c,b ), (b,a,c ), (b,c,a ), (c,a,b ), 
(c,b,a )}. For given n numbers there are n! different 
permutations.  
1Algorithm Perm( a,k,n ) 
2{ 
3   if (k=n) then write (a[1:n]);  
4   else 
5        for i:=k to n do  
6        { 
7           t:=a[k];a[k]:=a[ i];a[i]:=t; 
8           Perm(a,k+1,n);  
9           t:=a[k];a[k]:=a[ i];a[i]:=t; 
10         } 
11   } 
 
Performance Analysis  
•Space  Complexity  of an algorithm  is the 
amount  of memory  it needs  to run to 
completion . 
•Time  Complexity  is the amount  of computer  
time  it needs  to run to completion . 
•Performance  Evaluation  is divided  into two 
major  phases : 
–A priori  estimates  (performance  analysis)  
–A posteriori  testing  (performance  measurement)  
5/30/2017  
6 •Space Complexity:  
–Space needed is sum of following components:  
•Fixed  part that is independent  of characteristics  of inputs  
and outputs  (instance  characteristics) . For eg. Space  for 
code,  space  for constants . 
•Variable  part consists  of space  needed  by variables  whose  
size is dependent  on particular  problem  instance . 
•S(P) = c+Sp  where  c is constant  and Sp depends  on instance  
characteristics . Focus  is basically  on Sp (instance  
characteristics) . It is also important  to determine  which  
instance  characteristics  to use to measure  space  
requirements . 
•Example : 
   1.  Algorithm abc(a,b,c ) 
       2.  { 
       3.      return a+b+b *c+( a+b-c)/(a+b)+4.0;  
       4.   }  
        Space needed by this algorithm is independent of instance 
characteristics so Sp=0  
 
•Example 2:  
1. Algorithm Sum( a,n) 
2. { 
3.    s:=0.0;  
4.    for i:=1 to n do  
5.        s:=s+a[i]; 
6.    return s;  
7. } 
This problem  instance  is characterized  by n. n, s and i  are using  one 
word . Array  a is using  >= n words . So Ssum(n) >= (n+3) 
• Example  3: 
    1.   Algorithm  Rsum (a,n) 
   2.   { 
 3.       if (n<= 0) then  return  0.0; 
     4.       else return  Rsum (a,n-1)+a[n] ; 
  5. } 
This problem  instance  is characterized  by n. Recursion  stack  space  
includes  space  for formal  parameters,  local  variables  and return  address . 
Each  call requires  atleast  three  words  (for n, return  address  and pointer  
to a[]) As depth  of recursion  is n so space  needed  is >= 3n 
 
5/30/2017  
7 •Time Complexity:  
–Time  T(P) taken  by a program  P is sum  of compile  time  
and run time . As compile  time  does  not depend  on 
instance  characteristics  so focus  is on run time  
denoted  by t(p).  
–One way to calculate  run time  is to add additions,  
multiplications,  compares  etc. 
•Tp(n) = caADD(n)+ csSUB(n)+cmMUL (n)……………  
•It is impossible  to obtain  such  an exact  formula . 
–Another  way is to count  number  of program  steps  
(meaningful  segment  of a program  that has an 
execution  time) .  
–Return  a+b+b *c+( a+b-c)/(a+b)+4.0 can be regarded  as 
one step . 
–Number  of steps  any program  statement  is assigned  
depends  on kind  of statement . A comment  can be 
assigned  as zero  steps,  assignment  statement  as one 
step  and so on. 
•One way to determine  number  of steps  is to 
introduce  count  (initialized  to zero)  in the 
program . 
–Example : 
1Algorithm  Sum( a,n) 
2{ 
3   s:=0.0; 
4   count :=count  +1; 
5   for i:=1 to n do 
6   { 
7       count :=count+ 1;//For  for i 
8       s:=s+a[i]; count  := count+ 1// For assignment  
9    } 
10    count :=count+ 1 //For  last time  of for 
11    count :=count+ 1;//For  return  
12    return  s; 
13} 
 
 
5/30/2017  
8 –Simplified Algorithm  
1Algorithm Sum( a,n) 
2{ 
3    for i:=1 to n do count:=count+2;  
4    count:=count+3;

The Greedy Method  
•In some type of problems, we have n inputs and we are required to obtain a 
subset that satisfies some constraints.  
•Any subset that satisfies these constraints is called a feasible solution.  
•A feasible solution that either maximizes or minimizes a given objective 
function is called optimal solution.  
•Greedy method suggests that an algorithm can be devised that works in stages 
considering one input at a time. At each stage, a decision is made whether a 
particular input is in an optimal solution. This is done by including the next 
input into the partially constructed optimal solution and checking whether the 
inclusion results in an infeasible solution? If yes, that input is not added 
otherwise it is included.  
•Selection procedure for selecting next input is based on some optimization 
measure.  
•This version of greedy technique is called ‘subset paradigm’.  
•When we make decisions by considering the inputs in some order, that greedy 
technique is called ‘ordering paradigm’.

•An optimal  sequence  of decisions  has the property  that 
whatever  the initial  state  and decisions  are, the remaining  
decisions  must  constitute  an optimal  decision  sequence  with  
regard  to the state  resulting  from  the first decision . 
•In the greedy  method  only  one decision  sequence  is generated .

generated . Sequences  containing  suboptimal  subsequences  can 
not be optimal  so will not be generated .

is defined  by vertex  i1 to find path  from  i1 to j. Sequence  
i1,i2,i3…..ik,j must  constitute  shortest  path  from  i1 to j.

in V. The cost of a tour  is the sum  of the cost of the 
edges  on the tour. The TSP problem  is to find a tour  of 
minimum  cost.

there  are no known  polynomial  time  algorithms  are 
computationally  related . 
208 •A problem  which  is NP complete  has the property  that it 
can be solved   in  polynomial  time  iff all other  NP – 
complete  problems  can be solved  in polynomial  time .  
•If an NP-hard  problem  can be solved  in polynomial  time,  
then  all NP-complete  problems  can be solved  in polynomial  
time . 
•All NP-complete  problems  are NP-hard  but some  NP-hard  
problems  are not known  to be NP-complete . 
•Conclusion  : No NP-complete  or NP-hard  problem  is 
polynomially  solvable .

105 209 DETERMINISTIC and  NONDETERMINISTIC  
ALGORITHMS  
•Algorithms  having  the property  that the result  of every  operation  
is uniquely  defined   are called  deterministic  algorithms . Programs  
are executed  on a computer  in this way. 
•In theory,  some  algorithms  are allowed  that contain  operations   
whose  outcome  is not uniquely  defined  but  is limited   to a 
specified  set  of possibilities . Such  algorithms  are called  non-
deterministic  algorithms .  
•The machine  executing  such  operations  are allowed  to choose  any 
one of these  outcomes  subject  to a termination  condition . 
•Following  three  functions  are used  in non-deterministic  algorithms   
–Choice(S)  : arbitrarily  chooses  one of the elements  of set S. There  is no rule 
specifying  how  this choice  is to be made . 
–Failure()  : signals  an unsuccessful  completion . 
–Success()  : signals  a successful  completion . 
210 •A non-deterministic  algorithm  terminates  unsuccessfully  if and 
only  if there  exists  no set of choices  leading  to a success  signal . 
•Computing  times  for Choice,  Success  and Failure  are taken  to be 
O(1). 
•A machine  capable  of executing  a nondeterministic  algorithm  is 
called  a non-deterministic  machine  which  do not exist  in practice . 
•Example 1: Searching  an element  x in an array  A[1:n] 
1.j:=Choice( 1,n) 
2.If A[j]=x  then  { write  (j); Success() ;} 
3.write( 0); Failure() ; 
 Complexity  of this algorithm  is O(1). Every  deterministic  search  
algorithm  is of complexity  Ω(n). 
 
 
5/30/2017  
106 •Example 2: Sorting  in increasing  order . 
 Algorithm  Nsort (A,n) 
 { for i:=1 to n do B[i]:=0; 
  for i:=1 to n do 
  { j:=Choice( 1,n); 
   if B[j]≠ 0 then  Failure() ; 
   B[j]:=A[i]; 
  } 
  for i:=1 to n-1 do 
   if B[i]>B[i+ 1] then  Failure() ; 
  write  (B[1:n]); 
  Success() ; 
 } 
 Its complexity  is O(n) . All deterministic  sorting  algorithms  have  
complexity  Ω(nlogn ) 
 211 
•A deterministic  interpretation  of a non-deterministic  algorithm  
can be made  by allowing  unbounded  parallelism  in computation . 
Each  time  a choice  is to be made,  algorithms  makes  several  copies  
of itself . One copy  for each  of the possible  choices . First  copy  to 
reach  successful  completion  terminates  all other  computations . If 
a copy  reaches  failure  then  only  that copy  terminates . 
•A non-deterministic  machine  does  not make  any copies  of an 
algorithm  every  time  a choice  is to be made . 
•Any problem  for which  the answer  is either  zero  or one is called  
decision  problem .  
•An algorithm  for a decision  problem  is termed  as a decision  
algorithm . 
•Any problem  that involves  the identification  of an optimal  value  
of a given  cost function  is known  as an optimization  problem .  
•An optimization  algorithm  is used  to solve  an optimization  
problem . 
 
212

is made  if and only  if the output  is1. A 0 is output  if and only  if

completion . 
•Many  optimization  problems  can be recast  into decision  problems  
with  the property  that the decision  problem  can be solved  in 
polynomial  time  iff the corresponding  optimization  problem  can. 
•In other  cases,  if the decision  problem  cannot  be solved  in 
polynomial  time,  then  the optimization  problem  cannot  either . 
•Example 3: Maximum  Clique :  
–A maximal  complete  subgraph  of a graph  G=(V,E)  is a clique . Size of clique  is 
the number  of vertices  in it. 
–Max  Clique  problem  is an optimization  problem  that has to determine  the 
size of largest  clique  in G. Corresponding  decision  problem  is to determine  
whether  G has a clique  of size k. Suppose  DClique(G,k)   is a deterministic  
decision  algorithm  for Clique  decision  problem . If n is the number  of 
vertices  in G, then  size of max  clique  can be found  by executing  Dclique  for 
each  value  of k=n,  n-1, …….. If time  complexity  of DClique  is f(n) then  
optimization  problem  can be solved  in time  <=nf(n) . Also  if the optimization  
problem  can be solved  in time  g(n),  then  decision  problem  can also be 
solved  in time  g(n). So optimization  problem  can be solved  in polynomial  
time  iff decision  problem  can be solved  in polynomial  time . 
 
•Non -deterministic Algorithm for Clique decision problem:  
 Algorithm DCK(G,n,k)  
 { S:=Ǿ;  
  for i:=1 to k do  
  { t:=Choice(1,n);  
   if t Є S then Failure();  
   S:=S U {t};  
  } 
  for all pairs (i,j) such that i Є S, j Є S and i ≠ j do  
   if (i,j) is not an edge of G then Failure();  
  Success();  
 }

110 219 Classes NP -hard and NP -complete  
•P is the set of all decision  problems  solvable  by deterministic  
algorithms  in polynomial  time . 
•NP is the set of all decision  problems  solvable  by nondeterministic  
algorithms  in polynomial  time . 
•Since  deterministic  algorithm  are a special  case  of non 
deterministic  algorithms,  we can conclude  that PNP.  
•The most  famous  unsolved  problem  in computer  science  is 
whether  P = NP or P  NP. Is it possible  that for all the problems  in 
NP there  exist  polynomial  time  deterministic  algorithms  which  
have  remained  undiscovered  ? Till now  assumption  is P  NP. 
                NP P 
220 •S.COOK  formulated  the following  question  : 
•Is there  any single  problem  in NP such  that if we showed  it to be in 
P then  that would  imply  that P = NP? Cook  answered  his own  
question  in positive . 
•COOK’s  Theorem  : Satisfiability  is in P if and only  if P = NP. 
•Reducibility  
–Let L1 and L2 be problems . L1 reduces  to L2 (L1  L2) if and only  if there  is a 
way to solve  L1 by a deterministic  polynomial  time  algorithm  using  a 
deterministic  algorithm  that solves  L2 in polynomial   time . 
–If L1   L2 and L2   L3 then  L1   L3. 
•NP-Hard  Problem  : A problem  L is NP-hard  if any only  if 
satisfiability  reduces  to L (satisfiability   L). 
•NP-Complete : A problem  is NP-complete  if an only  if L is NP-hard  
and L Є NP.

222 •Example  :  
•Halting  problem  is NP-hard  decision  problem,  but it is not NP-
complete . 
Halting  Problem  :  
•To determine  for an arbitrary  deterministic  algorithm  A and an 
input  I whether  algorithm  A with  input  I ever  terminates  (or 
enters  an infinite  loop) . 
•Halting problem is un -decidable.  
•Hence there exists no algorithm to solve this problem.  
–So, it is not in NP .  
–So, it is not NP -complete.  
•To show  that Halting  problem  is NP-hard,  we show  that 
satisfiability   halting  problem . 
•For this let us construct  an algorithm  A whose  input  is a 
prepositional  formula  X. Suppose  X has n variables . Algorithm  A 
tries  out all 2n possible  truth  assignments  and verifies  if X is 
satisfiable . 
 
 
5/30/2017  
112 223 •If it is then  A stops .

•Hence  A halts  on input  iff X is satisfiable . 
•If we had a polynomial  time  algorithm  for the halting  problem,  
then  we could  solve  the satisfiability  problem  in polynomial  
time  using  A and X as input  to the algorithm  for the halting  
problem   
•Hence  satisfiability    halting  problem .  
•Hence the halting problem is an NP -hard problem which is not 
in NP  
•Thus Halting problem is NP -hard, but not NP -complete

instance  I’ of L2 from  any instance  I of L1 such  that from  the

– Satisfiability   L2

•A problem which is NP hard can not be solved in 
deterministic polynomial time.  
•Some restricted versions of NP hard problems can be 
solved in deterministic polynomial time.

hard. If each clause is restricted to have at most two literals,

•Create, control, verify and validate project 
deliverables
•Manage risks and implement risk response 
activities
•Manage sellers
•Adapt approved changes into the project’s scope, 
plans and environment
12
Project plan execution contd..
•Establish and manage project communication 
channels both external and internal to the 
project team
•Collect project data and  report cost, schedule, 
technical and quality progress and status 
information  to facilitate forecasting
•Collect and document lessons learned and 
implement approved process improvement 
activities
13
Project plan execution contd..
•Information about thecompletion status ofthe
deliverables andwhat hasbeen accomplished
iscollected asapartofproject execution andis
fedintotheperformance reporting process
•Though theproducts, services orresults ofthe
project arefrequently intheform oftangible
benefits asbuildings, roads etc, intangible
deliverables astraining canalsobeprovided
14
Project plan execution contd..
•Project plan execution also requires
implementation ofthefollowing
•Approved corrective actions that will bring
anticipatory project performance into
compliance with project management plan
•Approved preventive actions toreduce the
probability ofpotential negative consequences
•Approved defect repair requests tocorrect
product defects found bythequality process
15
Project scope management
•Project scope management (PSM) is 
concerned with defining and controlling what 
is and what is not included in the project
•PSM includes the processes required to ensure 
that the project includes all the work required 
to complete the project successfully
16
Project scope management contd..
•PSM includes the following
•Scope planning :Creating aplan thatdocuments how
theproject scope willbedefined, verified, controlled
andhow thework breakdown structure (WBS) will
becreated anddefined
•Scope definition :Developing ascope statement as
thebasis forfuture project decisions
•Create work breakdown structure :Subdividing the
major project deliverables and project work into
smaller, more manageable components
•Scope verification :Formalizing acceptance ofthe
completed project deliverables
17
Project scope management contd..
•Scope control :Controlling changes totheproject scope
•Scope planning :Defining and managing theproject
scope influences project’s overall success
Theproject scope management plan isadocument that
describes project scope, detailed project scope statement,
define and develop WBS, verify and control project
scope
•Detailed Scope definition :Thedetailed scope statement
depends onmajor deliverables, assumptions, constraints,
stakeholder needs andexpectations
Itisarefinement ofpreliminary project scope statement
asmore information about theproject isknown
The assumptions andconstraints areanalysed andmore
assumptions andconstraints areadded asnecessary
18
Project Scope Statement
•Project scope statement (PSS) describes the project’s 
deliverables and objectives and also the work required 
to create those deliverables
•The degree and level of detail PSS defines the work 
to be performed and the work to be excluded can 
determine how well the project management team can 
control the overall project scope
•The detailed PSS includes directly or indirectly the 
following documents
Project Objectives: It Includes business, cost, schedule, 
technical and quality objectives
19
Project Scope Statement contd..
Product scope description : Describes the
characteristics oftheproduct, service orresult that
theproduct wasundertaken tocreate
Project Requirements :Describes theconditions or
capabilities thatmust bemetbythedeliverables
Stakeholder needs, andexpectations aretranslated into
prioritized requirements
Project Boundaries :Itstates what isincluded inthe
project and explicitly states what isexcluded from
theproject ;otherwise thestakeholder might assume
thataparticular product, service orresult could bea
component oftheproject
20
Project Scope Statement contd..
•Project deliverables :Depending ontheproject scope
statement, the deliverables are described ata
summary level oratagreat detail
•Product acceptance criteria :Defines theprocess
andcriteria foraccepting completed products
•Process constraints :More detailed than the
constraints included intheproject charter ;schedule
milestones, predefined budget or contractual
provisions etc.
•Project assumptions :The assumptions are more
detailed than intheproject charter
21
Project assumptions contd..
•The assumptions include
Project organization
Defined risk
Schedule milestones
Fund limitation
Cost estimate
Project configuration management requirements
Change control
Project specifications
Project approval requirements
22
Work Breakdown Structure
•WBS isadeliverable oriented hierarchical
decomposition ofthework tobeexecuted bythe
project team toaccomplish theproject objectives and
create therequired deliverables
•The WBS subdivides theproject work into smaller,
more manageable anddetailed pieces ofwork
•Decomposition ofthetotal project work generally
involves thefollowing activities
-Identifying thedeliverables andrelated work
-Structuring andorganizing theWBS
23
Work Breakdown Structure contd..
-Decomposing the upper WBS levels into lower level 
detailed components
-Developing and assigning identification codes  to the 
WBS components
-Verifying that the degree of decomposition of the 
work is necessary and sufficient
•The resulting WBS can take a number of forms
-Using the major deliverables and subprojects as the 
first level of decomposition
-Using subprojects as the first level of 
decomposition, the subprojects may be contracted 
out;  the contractor applies WBS to contracted work
24
Work Breakdown Structure contd..
•Using the phases of the project life cycle as the first 
level of decomposition, the project deliverables 
inserted at the second level  
•Example WBS for defence aircraft system
Aircraft system
Training            Air vehicle           Data          Test and Evaluation 
Equipment TR   Airframe       Technical data         Mockups
Facility TR       Engine           Engineering data   Operational Test
Service TR    Communication system   MgMt data   Development
Navigation system                              Test
Fire control system
25

title: 7f7fb32a5480b01c
text:
Processes of a Project
Introduction
•Project Management isthe application of
knowledge, skills, tools andtechniques toproject
activities tomeet project objectives
•Itisaccomplished through processes using
knowledge, skills, tools and techniques with the
received inputs andgenerate outputs
•Aprocess isasetofinterrelated actions and
activities that areperformed toachieve apre-
specified setofproducts, results orservices
1
Processes  contd..
•Theproject processes areperformed bytheproject team
andcanbecategorized athigh level intotwotypes
•Processes associated with each other by their
performance foranintegrated purpose ;this type are
common tomost projects
•Product oriented processes specify and create the
project’s product ;they vary depending on the
application
•Both ofthe above type ofprocesses overlap and
interact ;forexample todefine thescope oftheproject,
understanding ofhow tocreate theproduct isrequired
2
Process groups
•Processes canbedivided into different groups in
terms oftheintegration between theprocesses,
theinteraction within them andthepurposes they
serve
•Initiating process groups
•Planning process groups
•Executing process groups
•Monitoring andcontrolling process groups
•Closing process groups
3
Initiating process groups
•This group consists ofprocesses thatfacilitate the
formal authorization tostart anew project ora
project phase
•Thegroup includes thefollowing processes
1.Develop Process Charter
Initial assumptions, decisions made and
constraints aredocumented inprocess charter
The project charter links the project tothe
ongoing work oftheorganization andauthorizes
theproject
4
Initiating process groups contd..
2. Develop Preliminary Project Scope
•This process is responsible for producing 
preliminary high level definition of the project
•Documents are made for the following
-project and deliverable requirements
-product requirements
-boundaries of the project
-methods of acceptance
-high level scope control     
5
Planning Process Group
•Includes thefollowing Project Management processes
1.Develop Project Management Plan
This process isresponsible for planning, executing,
monitoring, controlling andclosing oftheproject
2.Scope planning
This process isneeded forcreating aproject scope
management plan thatincludes
-scope definition, verification, control
-work breakdown structure creation anddefinition
3.Scope Definition
Necessary fordeveloping adetailed project scope
statement which isthebasis forfuture scope decision
6
Planning Process Group contd..
4.Create work breakdown structure
Itisused forsubdividing the major project
deliverables, and project work into smaller and
more manageable components
5.Activity Definition
Identify the specific actions that need tobe
performed toproduce the various project
deliverables
6.Activity Sequencing
Identifying and documenting dependencies
among scheduled activities
7
Planning Process Group contd..
7.Activity Resource Estimation
Estimating thetype and quantities ofresources
required toperform each scheduled activity
8.Activity Duration Estimation
Estimating thenumber ofwork periods thatwill
beneeded tocomplete individual scheduled
activities
9.Schedule Development
Analyzing activity sequence, duration, resource
requirement andschedule constraints tocreate the
project schedule
8
Planning Process Group contd..
10. Cost Estimating
Developing an approximation of the costs of the 
resources needed to complete project activities
11. Cost Budgeting
Aggregating the estimated costs of the individual 
activities or work packages to establish a cost 
baseline
12. Quality Planning
Indentifying which quality standards are relevant 
to the project and determining how to satisfy them
9
Planning Process Group contd..
13.Human Resource Planning
Identifying and documenting project roles,
responsibilities, andreporting relationships and
alsocreating thestaffing management plan
14.Communications Planning
Determining the information and
communication needs of the project
stakeholders
15.Risk Management Planning
Deciding how toapproach, plan, andexecute
theriskmanagement activities foraproject
10
Planning Process Group contd..
16.Risk Identification
Determining which risks might affect the
project anddocumenting their characteristics
17.Qualitative Risk Analysis
Forprioritizing risks forsubsequent analysis
oraction byassessing and combining the
probability ofoccurrence andimpact
18.Quantitative Risk Analysis
For numerically analyzing the effect on
overall project objectives ofidentified risks
11
Planning Process Group contd..
19.Risk Response Planning
For developing options and actions toenhance
opportunities and toreduce threats toproject
objectives
20.Plan Purchases andAcquisitions
Fordetermining what topurchase, oracquire and
determining when andhow
21.Plan Contracting
Fordocumenting products, services and results
requirements andidentifying potential sellers
12
3. Executing Process Group
•Consists ofprocesses used tocomplete the
work defined intheproject management plan
toaccomplish theproject objectives
•Theprocesses inthisgroup areasfollows
1.Direct andManage Project Execution
Directing the various technical and
organizational interfaces that exist inthe
project toexecute thework defined inthe
project management plan
13
Executing Process Group contd..
2.Perform Quality Assurance
Applying the planned, systematic quality
activities toensure that theproject employs all
processes needed tomeet requirements
3.Acquire Project Team
Obtaining the human resources needed to
complete theproject
4.Develop Project Team
Improving thecompetencies andtheinteractions
ofthe team members toenhance project
performance
14
Executing Process Group contd..
5.Information Distribution
Making information available to project
stakeholders inatimely manner
6.Request Seller Responses
Obtaining information, quotations, bids, offers or
proposals
7.Select sellers
Reviewing offers, choosing from among potential
sellers andnegotiating awritten contract with the
seller
15
4. Monitoring and Controlling Process Group
•Itconsists oftheprocesses thatareperformed to
observe project execution toidentify potential
problems intime sothatcorrective action canbe
taken tocontrol theexecution oftheproject
•Itconsists ofthefollowing processes
1.Monitor andcontrol project work
Collecting, measuring and disseminating
performance information, assessing progress,
andriskmonitoring
Performance reports provide information onthe
project with respect toscope, schedule, cost,
resource, quality andrisk
16
Monitoring and Controlling Process Group contd.. 
2.Integrated Change Control
Controlling factors thatcreate changes tomake
sure those changes are beneficial and
managing approved changes
This process isperformed throughout theproject
from initiation toclosure
3.Scope Verification
This process formalizes acceptance ofthe
completed project deliverables
17
Monitoring and Controlling Process Group contd.. 
4.Scope Control
This process isnecessary for controlling
changes totheproject scope
5.Schedule Control
Controlling changes toproject schedule
6.Cost Control
Influencing thefactors that create variances and
controlling changes totheproject budget
18
Monitoring and Controlling Process Group contd.. 
7.Perform Quality Control
Monitoring specific project result todetermine
whether they comply with relevant quality
standards and identifying ways toeliminate
causes ofunsatisfactory performance
8.Manage Project Team
Tracking team member performance providing
feedback, resolving issues, and coordinating
changes toenhance project performance
19
Monitoring and Controlling Process Group contd.. 
9.Performance Reporting
This process isnecessary forcollecting and
distributing performance information
It includes status reporting, progress
measurement andforecasting
10.Manage Stakeholders
Manage communications tosatisfy the
requirements ofand resolve issues with
project stakeholders
20
Monitoring and Controlling Process Group contd.. 
11.Risk Monitoring andControl
Tracking identified risks, monitoring residual
risks, identifying new risks, executing risk
response plan, and evaluating their effectiveness
throughout theproject lifecycle
12.Contract Administration
This process isnecessary for managing the
contract and relationship between thebuyer and
seller
Reviewing and documenting how aseller is
performing orperformed
21
5. Closing Process Group
•This group includes theprocesses needed toformally
terminate allactivities ofaproject oraproject phase
•Itincludes thefollowing processes
1.Close Project
This isnecessary tofinalize allactivities across allofthe
process groups toformally close aproject oraproject
phase
2.Contract Closure
This isnecessary for completing and settling each
contract
•Alloftheabove processes may notbeneeded forall
projects
22
Process Interactions
•The Process Groups are linked by the
objectives they produce
•The output ofoneprocess may betheinput of
another process ortheoutput isadeliverable of
theproject
•The Planning process group provides the
executing process group adocument project
management plan andproject scope statement
•Also updates theproject management plan as
theproject progresses
23
Process Interactions contd..
•The process groups arerarely discrete orone
time events
•They areoverlapping activities that occur at
varying levels ofintensity throughout the
project
•Ifthe project isdivided into phases, the
process groups interact within aproject phase
andalsomay across theproject phases
24
Project Milestones
•All projects will need tohave some fixed
milestones ortime boxes ifprogress towards a
planned delivery date istobemaintained
•The project customer orproject sponsor often
decides thekeyevents ormajor milestones for
thecompletion ofcertain deliverables bya
specified date
•The project manager decides the minor
milestones orthekey events fortheroutine
monitoring activities
25
Checkpoint Activities
•Sequencing activities for aproject involves
starting anew activity assoon asthepreceding
ones upon which itdepends have been completed
•Sometimes instead ofsequence ofactivities, the
project isdivided into stages and checkpoint
activities areintroduced
•These checkpoint activities which arethekey
activities represent thecompletion ofimportant
stages oftheproject
•Thecheck point activities areoften used asuseful
milestones
26
Major Milestones, Minor Milestones, Periodic Status 
Assessments
•The four Major Milestones occur atthe
transition points between lifecycle phases
•Inception, Elaboration, Construction,
Transition
•Thefour types ofmajor milestones are
1.Life cycle objectives Milestone
2.Life cycle Architecture Milestone
3.Initial Operational Capacity Milestone
4.Product Release Milestone
27
Life cycle objectives Milestone
•The goal istopresent toallstakeholders a
recommendation onhow toproceed with
development including aplan, estimated cost
andschedule andexpected benefits
•Asuccessfully completed lifecycle objectives
milestone will result inauthorization from all
stakeholders
28
Life cycle Architecture Milestone
•The primary goal istodemonstrate an
executable architecture toallstakeholders
•Amore detailed plan forconstruction phase is
presented forapproval
•A successfully completed Life cycle
Architecture Milestone will result in
authorization from stakeholders toproceed
with theconstruction phase
29
Life cycle Architecture Milestone contd..
•The content of the milestone should include 
the following
•An overview of the current present state
•A configuration controlled set of information 
available electronically or in hard copy
•An executable demonstration of capability
30
Initial Operational Capability Milestone
•The goals aretoassess thereadiness ofthe
software to begin the transition into
customer/user sites andtoauthorize thestart
ofacceptance testing
•Issues areaddressed concerning installation
instructions, software version descriptions user
andoperator manuals etc.
•Software quality metrics are reviewed to
determine whether quality issufficient for
transition
31
Product Release Milestone
•The Product Release Milestone occurs atthe
endofthetransition phase
•The goal istoassess thecompletion ofthe
software and itstransition tothe support
organization
•The results ofacceptance testing arereviewed
andallopen issues areaddressed
32
Minor Milestones
•The number ofinformal milestones needed
depends onthecontent and length ofthe
iteration ortasks
•Formost iterations which have one-month to
six-month duration, only twominor milestones
areneeded :theiteration readiness review and
theiteration assessment review
33
Iteration Readiness Review
•This informal milestone isconducted atthe
start ofeach iteration toreview thedetailed
plan and theevaluation criterion that have
been allocated
•Iteration Assessment Review :This informal
milestone isconducted attheend ofeach
iteration toassess thedegree towhich the
iteration achieved itsobjectives and satisfied
itsevaluation criteria
34
Periodic Status Assessments
•Managing risks requires continuous attention to
allthe interacting activities ofasoftware
development effort
•Periodic Status Assessments are management
reviews conducted atregular intervals (monthly,
quarterly) toaddress progress and quality
indicators, ensure continuous attention toproject
dynamics, and maintain open communications
among allstakeholders
•Theimportant objective ofthese assessments isto
ensure that theexpectations ofallstakeholders
aresynchronized andconsistent
35
Periodic Status Assessments contd..
•Status assessments provide thefollowing
•A mechanism for openly addressing,
communicating, and resolving management
issues, technical issues, andproject risks
•Objective data derived directly from ongoing
activities andevolving product configurations
•Amechanism for disseminating process,
progress, quality trends, practices, and
experience information toand from all
stakeholders inanopen forum
36
Additional Reference
•Walker Royce, Software Project Management 
A Unified Framework,  Pearson Education
37

title: 4fd046cd66fd6172
text:
Project management Framework: PRINCE2
•PRINCE 2 (an acronym for PRojects IN
Controlled Environments) isadefacto process -based
methodology orframework for effective project
management
•Used extensively bytheUKGovernment, PRINCE 2
isalso widely recognised andused intheprivate sector,
both intheUKandinternationally
•ThePRINCE 2method isinthepublic domain, (which
hasCrown copyright) andoffers non-proprietorial best
practice guidance onproject management1
Key features of PRINCE2
•Focus onbusiness justification
•Defined organisation structure fortheproject
management team
•Product -based planning approach
•Emphasis ondividing theproject into
manageable andcontrollable stages
•Flexibility thatcanbeapplied atalevel
appropriate totheproject .
2
PRINCE2 History
•PRINCE was originally based onPROMPT, a
project management method created bySimpact
Systems Ltdin1975
•Itwas adopted asthestandard tobeused forall
Government information system projects
•PRINCE was launched in1989 ,andsuperseded
PROMPT within Government projects
•PRINCE 2was published in1996 and was
contributed byaconsortium ofsome 150
European organisations .
3
Benefits of PRINCE2
•Provides greater control of resources, and the ability 
to manage business and project risk more effectively
Who can be benefited?
•Individuals seeking leading project management skills 
and greater employment prospects
•Project managers
•Directors/executives (senior responsible owners) of 
projects, and
•Organisations
4
Benefits contd..
•For organisations , it provides
A common, consistent approach,
A controlled and organised start, middle 
and end
Regular reviews of progress against plan
Assurance that the project continues to 
have a business justification
www.prince2.com
5
PRINCE2 Components
•Organization
•Planning
•Controls
•Stages
•Management of Risk
•Quality
•Configuration Management
•Change Control
6
PRINCE2 Planning Technique
•PL1  Design a plan
• PL2  Define and Analyse Products
• PL3  Identify Activities and their 
Dependencies
• PL4  Estimate effort for each activity
• PL5  Schedule
• PL6  Analyse Risk
• PL7  Complete plan
7
PRINCE2 Project Organization
PRINCE 2isbased ontheassumption that the
project willinvolve
•Users oftheproducts oftheproject
•Suppliers ofgoods andservices needed forthe
project
users andsuppliers could belong tothesame
organization, butforbetter management and
control purpose they aredistinguished
8
PRINCE2 Project Organization contd..
•Customer side there are two roles –executive 
role and user role
•The executive role has to ensure that the 
project continues to meet the business 
requirements
•User role is to actually use the system on a day 
to day basis
•Executive, supplier and user constitute Project 
Board 
9
PRINCE2 Project Organization contd..
•Thetask ofmanaging theproject onaday-to-day
basis will bedelegated bytheProject Board to
theProject Manager
•Onalarge project, Project Manager may delegate
certain aspects oftheproject tospecialist Team
Managers
•The Project Manager can require support of
administrative staff (project support staff), for
example tokeep track oflatest versions oftools
etc.
10
Project Management Team
•TheProject Board
•Project Manager
•Team Leaders
•Project Assurance andSupport Staff
11
Project Stages
•A large project may be divided into stages.
•One or more phases of project development can be a 
stage
•Project Manger can start a new stage only when the 
Project Board approves the current stage
•Each stage has a stage plan
•Project Board receives regular reports from the 
Project Manager
•Due to any problem the stage plan could not be 
executed , the Project Board can terminate the project 
permanently
12
Project Procedures
•Major PRINCE2 processes
Prince ID              Major Processes
SU                  Starting up a project
IP                  Initiating a project
DP                 Directing a project
CS                Controlling a stage
MP                 Managing product delivery
SB                   Managing stage boundaries
CP                   Closing a project
PL                   Planning
13
Project Management Tools
Two commercial project management tools
And a Freeware
•Microsoft Project
•Oracle’s Primavera SureTrak
•GanttProject (freeware)
14
Important Features of Microsoft Project
•Support for Colloboration : It can be used with 
Internet, allowing team members to view various 
tasks assigned to them
•Portfolio view: The project manager can examine 
multiple projects simultaneously; how changes in 
one project can affect other projects
•Task Linking: Allows interlinking various tasks in a 
project, the effect of delay to one task on the 
other can be studied
15
Important Features of Microsoft Project contd..
•Resource Pooling :Resources aspeople,
equipment and materials can be shared
between projects using ashared resource pool
Each resource canbeassigned tomultiple tasks
and each task can beassigned multiple
resources
16
Project Management software: Primavera
•SureTrak isthebasic software andPrimavera 6
istheadvanced software
•Aproject manager candefine project phases,
establish goals, know the obstacles, and
delegate assignments
17
Features of Primavera
•Variable Timescale :Users canseesome portion
oftheproject plan indays andrestinweeks
•Scheduling Support :Activities canbeexamined
and impact ofchange toanactivity onthe
completion time oftheproject canbeviewed
•Highlight Specific Activity Attributes :Using
different patterns andcolors fordifferent activity
attributes, project manager can highlight
important aspects oftheproject
18
Features of Primavera contd..
•Web Interface :Allows theproject manager to
interact with team members ;reports and
documents published canbeviewed bymembers
•Cost Management :For project control cost
management and earned value analysis can be
performed
•Contractor Management :Some portions ofthe
project aregiven tosubcontractors
Allows tokeep track oftheir progress and
productivity
19
GanttProject
•AGantt chart isatype ofbar chart,
developed byHenry Gantt in1910 ,that
illustrates aproject schedule with thestart and
finish dates
•GanttProject isaJava based open source tool
initiated in2003 inaUniversity inFrance for
project management with limited features
20
Features of GanttProject
•Project Management
•GanttChart
•Resource Management
•Scheduling
•Project Portfolio Management (manage   
multiple projects)
•Task Hierarchies and Dependencies
•MS Project import / Export
•Exchange data with spreadsheet applications
•PDF and HTML reports
•Available in about 20 languages
21
Project stakeholders
•Individuals and organizations that areactively
involved intheproject
•Canbecategorized as
-Internal totheproject team who areunder the
direct control oftheproject manager
-External totheproject team butwithin thesame
organization (for example theproject manager
may usetheservices ofpeople forsystem testing
-External toboth the project team and the
organization (customers who benefit from the
project orthecontractors who carry outwork for
theproject)
22
Project stakeholders contd..
•Different stakeholders have different interests ;
end users need ease ofuse oftheproject,
managers areinterested inreducing thestaff
•The project manager hastomanage allthese
people
•Acommunication plan hastobecreated atthe
start oftheproject
23
Role of Project Manager
•Project managers can have the
responsibility oftheplanning, execution
andclosing ofanyproject
•Responsible forcompleting theproject
objectives
•Responsible for building the project
requirements, and managing the
constraints which
include cost, time, scope andquality .
24
Role of Project Manager contd..
•Project manager reports tochief executive ortheboard
consisting ofmembers
•Theproject team reports toproject manger
•Overall execution oftheproject
•Communicate with allstakeholders asand when
required
-sohe/she must have afair knowledge ofthe
organization and capable ofunderstanding and
discussing theproblems with clients and thehigher
authorities
•Generate various kinds ofreports
25

title: 2e150fc8393af320
text:
Problems with software projects
Problems related to project management
–unclear objectives
–Poor planning
–project management methodology correctly not 
followed
–Changing to new technology
–insufficient staff
•Effective project management is key to 
successfully executing a project
1
Problems with software projects contd..
•Problems with project planning 
2
Lack of Leadership
•A  talented and motivated team who are 
involved throughout the project can make a 
successful project.
3
Deviation from scope
•A change in project priorities due to lack of 
understanding of the scope of the project
•When customer needs are not well understood, 
wrong software is built
4
Communication gap
•There isacommunication gap between the
people who build thesoftware andthose who
need it.
•You can mitigate this problem byletting
people know the current progress on a
regular basis and when milestones are
accomplished orthestatus changes .
5
Fixing Planning Problems
–Use avision andscope document todefine
theneeds oftheusers andstakeholders
–Use aproject plan tokeep every one
informed about how those needs willbemet
–Useriskplanning tokeep theplan realistic
6
Problems with Project estimates and scheduling
•Aproject manager under pressure simply
imposes adeadline, and creates unrealistic
estimates thatmeet it
-Unrealistic estimates shorten thetasks in
theschedule orcutting them entirely until
everything fits
–When theschedule gets tight, any non-
programming activities are cut and the
software isreleased before it’sfinished
7
Problems with Project estimates and scheduling contd..
•Disconnected business priorities
There is often a wide gap between the 
priorities of projects within the development, 
organization and the priority of the project in 
the eyes of the requester. 
High priority project for one department is 
not viewed as important by the organization  
as many projects may be there for the 
organization
Everyone needs to be  the same  with  respect to 
Priorities 8
Problems with Project estimates and scheduling 
contd..
•Adding people to a project 
It may take only a few days or weeks for a 
developer to come into the project at the 
beginning, but it could take months for a 
developer to be fully productive when added to 
the project long after it has started
•Multi -tasking
The more you ask people to multi -task, the worse 
their work will be and the longer it will take. 
9
Fixing Scheduling Problems
–These canbeavoided byadopting good planning
and estimation practices and creating aproject
schedule
–Scheduling techniques like critical path analysis
canhelp spot problems early on
10
Review Problems
Problems Are Found Too Late
–The team may misunderstand a need, but that’s 
not discovered until delivery
Requirements may be missed or incorrect
–The design may be difficult to use or fail to take 
all of the features into account
11
Review Problems contd..
Long Meetings
–To solve some  persisting problem the project 
manager conducts long meetings; the meetings 
may end up without making any progress
Non availability of Indispensable persons
–Important persons like senior programmer may not 
be available to discuss the bugs
12
Fixing Review Problems
•Problems that arefound toolate, big meetings, and
the indispensable persons like programmer are
problems which canbesolved with reviews
–Reviews can catch defects early, when they are
cheaper tofix
–Areview meeting only includes the people
necessary forthework tobedone
–Reviews especially code reviews can help the
senior programmer spread his expertise and
knowledge
13
Problems with software projects
•People -related problems
•Process -related problems
•Product -related problems
•Technology -related problems
14
People -related problems
Low motivation :The project manager is
responsible forthelevel ofmotivation within
theteam .
Lengthy projects, complex activities and
scarce resources often decrease themotivation
level inasoftware development team
•The project manager has to constantly
motivate thepeople todoagood job.
15
People related problems contd..
•Problem employees :Some members ofany
team always create aproblem .They lower the
efficiency and productivity ofother team
members and make itdifficult tomeet the
objectives ofthesoftware project within the
specified time.
•The project Manager has toensure that
employees arenotallowed tocreate aproblem
fortherestoftheteam, even iftheemployee is
very competent
16
People related problems contd..
•Unproductive work environment :The work
environment isamajor factor that affects the
productivity ofthedevelopment team ;forexample,
anoisy orcramped workspace decreases the
motivation levels oftheemployees .
Similarly, unfriendly organizational policies also
lower themotivation oftheteam members .
Theproject manager needs toensure thattheteam
is
protected from such external disturbances and
make theworkspace friendly towork in.
17
People related problems contd..
•Inefficient project management style :the
project manager needs tolead byexample
•The team members absorb thework culture,
work ethic, andattitude oftheproject manager
andimplement itintheir work style .
•Ifhedisplays alack ofleadership qualities and
weak ideals, themotivation levels decrease
across software team .
18
People related problems contd..
•Lack ofstakeholder interest :Forasoftware
project tobeasuccess, each stakeholder needs to
take anactive interest intheprogress ofthe
project .
•All stakeholders, including the customer, the
management, andthesoftware development team,
need tocommit tothesuccess oftheproject .
•Ifthe software development team isnot
committed totheproject, then their contribution
may notbetotheoptimum level .
19
People related problems contd..
Ineffective project sponsorship by
management :Lack ofcommitment ofthe
senior management toasoftware project
lowers themotivation level oftheteam
members .
•Ifthemanagement commits totheprogress
ofasoftware project, and takes akeen
interest intheprogress, theconfidence of
the software development team will
increase .
20
Process -related Problems
Unrealistic schedule :Assigning unrealistic deadlines fora
software project is
aprimary reason why software projects aredelayed .Often,
themarketing orthemanagement team commit adelivery date
tothecustomer inthehope ofgetting theproject contract .
•However, these dates many times are not decided in
consultation with thedevelopment team .
•Itisessential toensure thatthedeadlines match theability of
thesoftware team todeliver thesoftware product .
•Asitisnotalways possible toshift deadlines committed tothe
customer, you also need toplan theresource allocation and
project execution such thatthedeadlines aremet.
21
Process -related Problems contd.. 
•Abandoning quality under pressure ofdeadlines :
Where asoftware project faces ashortage of
resources, time, andfunds,
project managers often push away quality concerns
andfocus onmeeting deadlines andstaying within the
budget .
•Abandoning quality adds even more time, effort, and
costs tothesoftware projects .
•The cost ofdoing things right thefirst time islower
than thecostofinspection during product delivery .
•Also, thecost ofinspection islower than thecost of
debugging software after thecustomer spots errors .
22
Process -related Problems contd.. 
•Unstructured andhurried software development :
When software project progresses with more focus on
meeting deadlines andstaying within abudget,
theapproach tothesoftware development isunstructured
andhurried .
•One should plan thesoftware project such that allthe
activities areidentified, sequenced properly, androles and
responsibilities assigned tothe various people onthe
project
• One should alsomaintain thefocus ofthedevelopment
team toward astructured approach to software
development .
23
Process -related Problems contd.. 
•Insufficient Risk identification: Unidentified, 
partially identified, and unplanned
risks pose a threat to the success of a software 
project. 
It is required to intensively identify risks and evolve 
a risk management plan such that the project is
completed successfully, on time
24
Process -related Problems contd.. 
•Unsuitable life cycle model selection : Different 
software projects require different SDLC models. For 
example, a project to create banking software is 
different from
software for a satellite where the concept needs to be
researched
•For the former example, the Waterfall model is more 
applicable
•For the latter example, the Spiral model is more 
suitable. 
•Selecting the correct life cycle model is critical to the 
success of a software project.
25
product -related problems
•Product scope changed towards theend oftheproject life
cycle :Theproject time, effort, andcostestimates forasoftware
project cangoupdramatically when thecustomer changes the
scope oftheproduct toward theendoftheproject .
•Insuch situations, thecriticality ofthescope change should
beverified
•Ifthechange request isnotcritical, theoriginal scope canbe
retained with aproper explanation tothecustomer .
•Ifthechange request iscritical, explain thesituation tothe
customer .
•Usually, acustomer gives more time andfunds toasoftware
project ifproper justification isprovided .
•Insome cases, thescope change may also bebecause ofa
change ingovernment policy ;itmay become mandatory for
youtoinclude such change requests .
26
Technology related problems
•Research -oriented software development :Many
software projects deviate from theoriginal scope because of
thenature ofthesoftware product ortechnology used
•When atotally new kind ofsoftware isdeveloped oranew
technology isused, thesoftware development team canlose
focus oftheobjectives bygetting into aresearch -oriented
approach
•Itbecomes theresponsibility oftheproject manager to
maintain thefocus ontheobjective
27
COST -BENEFIT ANALYSIS
Introduction
Feasibility study
•Operational feasibility is centered on human factors 
as is the problem worth solving ?  
•What are the clients expectations ?
Technical feasibility is concerned with respect to 
computer and hardware.
•Can the problem be solved on computer?
•Is the technology available? 
•Is expertise to use technology available?
28
Feasibility Contd.
Economic feasibility
•costs and benefits
•Early estimates based on heuristics
•Detailed estimates and cost -benefit analysis
Clients and analysts must evaluate the results of all the 
three analyses and make decisions based on that
COCOMO (Constructive Cost Model) is a cost model
Putnam Model is a resource estimation/effort estimation 
model
29
Cost benefit analysis
•Cost benefit analysis isasystematic approach to
estimate the economic feasibility ofasystem
considering theincurred costs and estimating the
return oninvestment
•Itinvolves System costs, and benefits from the
system .
• Ifthesystem iseconomically feasible means the
benefits outweigh thesystem costs within adefined
period oftime acceptable totheuser/client .
30
SYSTEM COSTS
1. Development costs: The following are some development 
costs
One time expense for 
the projectFurniture chairs etc. Facility costs (prepare 
facility to operate the 
system, AC etc.)
Personnel costs 
(salaries) etc.Computer usage 
costsMiscellaneous 
expenses (rent, utilities 
etc.)
User time Supply and materials 
costscorrespondence costs 
(Postal, shipping costs)
Training costs Peripherals, office 
supplies consumed
Equipment costs 
(hardware, software)Costs of manual and 
documents
31
System cost Contd…
2.    Ongoing Operating costs: recurring costs for operation 
of the system, maintenance costs etc.
3.  Fixed costs: occur at regular intervals as property taxes, 
lease payments
Company provides some benefits to employees as 
hospital, market etc.
4.  Variable costs : base on the usage of the system (CPU 
time, supply costs, wage costs, maintenance costs)
32
BENEFITS
Increase profits or decrease costs
1.Performance Benefits: 
•To improve quality of work or to start new activities
•Error reduction, speed of activity, access to new 
information etc.
2. Cost -Avoidance Benefits:
•Some clerical staff can be reduced due to new 
system
•Manual errors can be less due to more automation
33
Benefits contd..
3. Tangible Benefits:
•Can be estimated accurately
•Measures as monthly or annual savings
•Staff reduction
•Manufacturing a new part
4.Intangible benefits:
•Goodwill
•Environmental friendly
34
Quantifying  intangible benefits
•Method 1 : Subjective estimation
•User makes estimation based on experience
•Analysts document and add to cost -Benefit report
Method 2 : Decision Theory (based on expected values)
•Assign probabilities to various outcomes.
If better working conditions are provided, by what 
percentage people leaving company is reduced ? For eg. 
50 % chance of <4 % reduction
If less people leave the organization, savings in terms 
of  termination pay, recruitment cost  and training costs 
etc.
35
Quantifying  intangible benefits contd..
•Method 3 : Working backwards from desired results.
Better working conditions cost Rs. 100 000
Savings of a person not leaving Rs.   18 700   
Hence reduce (turnover of people) or people 
leaving by = ~5.35 people
(100 000 / 18700    = ~5.35)
36
COST -BENEFIT TERMINOLOGY
•Spending vs. Investment : Spending is purchasing what is 
needed for the operation of the system. Investment is the 
money spent and it can generate revenue. Goal is to 
maximize revenue.
•Direct versus Indirect Costs and Benefits : Direct cost and 
benefits are related to the system
Indirect costs and benefits are expenses and revenue that 
are shared with the other components of the organization. 
For eg. The director of an organization is involved in 
many projects.
37
COST -BENEFIT TERMINOLOGY Contd..
•Economic Life : Period of time the investment is expected 
to yield benefits.
-Residual value : the value of parts of the existing system 
that can be salvaged (relieved). 
-Required rate of Return : Minimum rate of return a 
company can accept on an investment.
•Sunk costs : Costs related to an investment which have 
already been paid out
Just because $ 20000 (sunk cost) has already been 
invested in a project, you cannot justify proceeding with 
the project .
38
Techniques Used to Determine Economic Feasibility
1.Payback Analysis
2.Return on Investment
3.Net Present Value
4.Profitability Index
The required inputs to apply the techniques are:
1.Development costs
2.Annual Operating Costs
3.Annual Benefits
4.Economic life of the system (5 yrs.)
5.Required rate of return (15%)
39
Techniques Used to Determine Economic Feasibility Contd..
1. Payback Analysis is to determine in how much time 
the accrued benefits overtake accrued costs. 
Breakeven point is when debts have been cancelled by 
benefits.
Payback period (T) =   Development   costs (D)
Annual Revenue -annual operational costs (P)
2. Internal Rate of Return (IRR) :  is a measure of 
relationship between investment in a project and net 
benefits from the project.  
IRR =  estimated lifetime benefits –estimated lifetime costs 
estimated life time costs
To calculate yearly IRR, divide  lifetime IRR by the 
economic life of the system.                                                       
40
Techniques Used to Determine Economic Feasibility Contd..
3. Present Value & Net Present Value (NPV)
Costs and benefits of the system are calculated in terms of 
today’s dollars (i.e. the value of the investment in today’s 
dollars)
NPV = Present value of total benefits –present value of
total costs
4. Profitability Index (PI)
Attempts to measure risk by determining ratio of present 
value of benefits to the development of costs.
PI =       present value of benefits
present value of development costs
41
Stages of a project: Main activities in Project Management
•Feasibility study  (Operational, Technical, and 
Financial)
Is it worth doing?
•Planning  (if feasible)
How do we do it?
•Execution  (implement the plan)
Do it
42
Main activities in Project Management contd..
•Feasibility study is performed for large and 
complex projects
•Planning is done before the main engineering 
Life cycle (LC) and closure after the LC
•Monitoring phase is in parallel with LC
43
Project Planning
•Basic objective: To create a plan to meet the 
commitments of the project, i.e. create a path 
that, if followed, will lead to a successful 
project
•Planning involves defining the Life Cycle (LC) 
process to be followed, cost and time 
estimates, detailed schedule, plan for quality, 
etc.
•Main output -a project management plan and 
the project schedule
44
Key Planning Tasks
•Define suitable processes for executing the 
project 
•Estimate effort
•Define project milestones and create a schedule
•Define quality objectives and a quality plan
•Identify risks and make plans to mitigate them
•Define measurement plan, project -tracking 
procedures, training plan, team organization, etc.
45
Process Planning
•Plan how the project will be executed, i.e. the 
process to be followed
•Process will decide the tasks, their ordering, 
milestones
•Hence process planning is an important project 
planning task 
•Should plan for LC and PM processes as well 
as supporting processes
46
Life Cycle Process
•Various LC models -waterfall, iterative, 
prototyping; diff models suit different projects
•During planning can select the model that is 
best for the project
•This gives the overall process which has to be 
fine-tuned to suit the project needs
•Usually done by process tailoring -changing 
the process to suit the project
•Tailoring finally results in adding, deleting, 
modifying some process steps
47

title: 41ae513cfeb287af
text:
Introduction to Software Project Management
Software
Project
Software Project
Engineering
Management
Software Engineering
Software Project Management
1
Introduction to Software Project Management contd..
•Software (IEEE): collection of programs, 
procedures, rules, and associated 
documentation and data 
•Project:  A Project is a temporary endeavor or 
effort undertaken to create a unique product, 
service or result 
2
Engineering
•The American Engineer’s Council forProfessional
Development hasdefined "engineering" as
The creative application ofscientific principles to
design ordevelop structures, machines, apparatus, or
manufacturing processes,
orworks utilizing them singly orincombination ;or
toconstruct oroperate thesame with fullcognizance
oftheir design ;ortoforecast their behaviour under
specific operating conditions ;allasrespects an
intended function, economics ofoperation orsafety to
lifeandproperty .
3
Management
•Management isthefunction thatcoordinates
the efforts ofpeople toaccomplish goals
and objectives using available resources
efficiently andeffectively .
•Management word isgenerally used with
respect tobusiness andorganizations
4
Management contd..
•Planning  -decides what is to be done
•Organizing  -making arrangements
•Staffing   -selecting the right people for the job
•Directing  -giving instructions
•Monitoring  -checking the progress
•Controlling  -taking action to remedy hold ups
•Innovating  -coming up with solutions when 
problems arise
•Representing  -liasoning (act as a link) with clients, 
users, developers and other stakeholders
5
Software Engineering
•s/wEngg .focuses ongeneral software
•s/wEngg .(IEEE) :systematic approach todevelopment, of
software operation, maintenance, andretirement ofsw
•Systematic approach :includes methodologies andpractices
thatcanbeused tosolve aproblem
•The problem ofproducing software tosatisfy user needs
drives theapproaches used inSE
6
Project Characteristics
•Temporary
Projects starts and ends 
Project is completed when the objectives are 
achieved
Examples
• Monument creation
• Artefacts Production
•Research Project  producing a document is   
useful for decision making
7
Project Characteristics contd..
•Duration   
(generally 6 months to 10 years)
2 or 3 years are very common time periods
•Uniqueness (Every project has different 
objectives)
•Scope   (can not be very general)
8
Project Characteristics contd..
•Can not be well defined in the beginning
(progressive elaboration is possible)
Work carried out for customers
•Large and complex projects involve many 
disciplines, and number of phases
•Time and Resource constraints
9
Difference between software projects and other projects
•Invisibility  (You may not see the result as a 
product)
•Complexity
•Conformity or consistency (scientific methods 
are followed)
•Flexibility  (can be modified easily)
10
Projects versus jobs
•Ajobisasequence ofspecific operations
•Ajobincludes anumber ofroutine tasks
•Each taskiswell defined andwell understood
•Uncertainty isnegligible
11
Software for Industry
•Others who have not developed the software 
are the users
•Requirements
–bugs not tolerated
–Good user Interface is required
–Documents needed for the user as well as 
for the organization and the project
12
Software for Industry contd..
•Supports important functions for business
•Reliability , robustness are very important
•Heavy investment
•Portability is a key issue
13
Software for Industry contd..
•Brooks thumb -rule:Industrial strength sw
costs 10times more than other sw
•Domain ofSWEngg :Industrial strength sw
•InSW Engg .and inthis course, software
means industrial strength software
14
Driving factors for software
Productivity  (the effectiveness of productive effort)
•An engineering project is driven by cost and schedule
•In s/w, cost is mainly manpower cost, hence 
measured in person -months
•Schedule is in months/weeks –very important in 
business context
•Productivity P captures both of these
–If P is higher, cost is lower
–If P is higher, time taken can be lesser
15
Driving factors for software contd..
Quality (Q)
•Developing high Q s/w is a basic goal
•Quality of s/w is harder to define
•Approaches used should produce a high Q 
software
16
Quality: ISO standard
•Requires six attributes
–Functionality
–Reliability
–Usability
–Efficiency
–Maintainability
–Portability
17
Reliability
•Reliability is generally considered the main 
Quality criterion
•Reliability  is a measure of of failure 
•= 1 -Probability  of failure
–hard to measure
–approximated by no. of defects in software
Basic approach ofSEistoseparate process
from products and focus onprocess and
managing theprocess
18
Software Project
•Goal :Build asoftware system tomeet
commitments oncost, schedule, quality
•Worldwide -many projects fail
–one-third areduetocostorschedule overrun
19
Project Management
•Project management isthe process and
activity ofplanning, organizing, motivating,
and controlling resources, procedures and
protocols toachieve specific goals inscientific
ordaily problems .
20
Objectives of a project
•Project Manager :Aproject istaken care bya
project in-charge ormanager (may beaperson
oragroup) who sets theproject scope and
allocates costs
•The group may beknown asaproject board,
management board orthesteering committee
•Focus ofproject manager orproject board ison
what will bedone rather than how itwill be
done
21
Objectives should be SMART
S    Specific, concrete and well defined
M   Measurable, Can be objectively judged
A     Achievable  (within the power of the 
individual or the group to meet the target)
R   Relevant to the purpose of the project
T   Time constrained  (within sometime the 
objectives should be achieved)
22
Goals or sub -objectives
•Steps toachieve objectives areknown asgoals
•Objective Xwill beachieved ifthe sub-
objectives orgoals A,B,Cetc.are all
achieved
•Goal canbeallocated toanindividual butnot
theobjective
23
Example of objective and goal 
Objective: User satisfaction with software product
Analyst goal: Accurate requirements
Developer goal: software that is reliable
Measures of effectiveness:  How do we know goals 
or objectives have been achieved?
By practical test they can be objectively assessed
For example, if the number of complaints are low 
and the customers buy more products, then user 
satisfaction is achieved
24
Formal Project Management
•Formal Project Management and Formal
Development methods play animportant role
intheexecution oflarge andcomplex projects
than small projects
•Formality :well defined processes used for
each task;measurements used tocontrol
25
Product definition
•Aproduct is the item offered for sale. A product can be a 
service or an item. It can be physical or in virtual or cyber 
form.
(economictimes.indiatimes.com)
•A good, idea, method ,object orservice created as a result of 
aprocess andserves aneed or satisfies a want.
•It has a combination oftangible andintangible 
attributes (benefits, features, functions and  uses that a seller 
offers a buyer for purchase). 
•For example a seller of a toothbrush not only offers the 
physical product but also the idea that the consumer will be 
improving the health of their teeth.
(http://www.businessdictionary.com)
26
Product Contd..
•A project when successfully completed  and 
made operational or converted into something 
useful is a product
•Categories of projects
-Information systems versus embedded 
systems
-Objective based  versus product based
27
References
1. Bob  Hughes and Mike Cotterell , Software Project management, 5rd
Edition, Tata McGraw Hill, 2013
2. A Guide to the Project management Body of Knowledge (PMBOK), 
Project Management Institute, PA, (2004) (e -Book available)
3. Walker Royce: Software Project management, Pearson Education, 2005
4. Pankaj Jalote , Software Project management in Practice, Pearson 
Education, 2005
5. James A O’Brien, George M Maracas, Ramesh Behl : Management 
Information Systems, McGraw Hill,  Tenth Edition, 2013
6. Roger S. Pressman, Software Engineering, A Practitioner’s Approach, 
McGraw Hill Education,  2010
7. Wouter Baars , Project management handBook , July 2006 (E -Book 
available)
8. Project management Guide Book (E -Book)  available at  www. 
Method123.com
9. Alexis Leon, Enterprise Resource Planning, Tata McGraw Hill, 2001
28

File Handling
•Introduction
•File Opening modes
•Opening and closing of a file
•Reading from a file
•Writing onto a file
•Error handling during I/O operations
•Record I/O in files
1
Introduction to files
•Programs are stored in memory i.e. Random access memory
But this storage is not permanent
•For permanent storage, it is required to use files to store programs and 
data and read them from there
•C language supports a number of functions to perform basic file 
operations
•A file is a collection of bytes that is stored on secondary storage 
devices like disk. There are two kinds of files in a system. They are,
•Text files (ASCII)
•Binary files
•Text files contain ASCII codes of digits, alphabets and symbols.
•Binary file contains collection of bytes (0’s and 1’s)
2
Difference between text files and binary files
•There are two kinds ofstoring data infile-text format and binary
format
•Intext file data are stored asline ofcharacters with each line
terminated byanew line character (‘\n’)
•Inbinary format data isstored onthe disk inthe same way asitis
represented inthe computer memory .Unix system does not make
anydistinction between text fileand binary file.
•Text files areinhuman readable form and they can becreated and
read using any text editor, while binary files are not inhuman
readable form and they can becreated and read only byspecific
program written forthem
3
Difference between text files and binary files contd..
•The binary data stored infile can not beread using text editor .The
hexadecimal value of1679 is0x068f,soinbinary format itisrepresented
bytwo bytes 0x06and 0x8f
•Inatext file1679 isrepresented bythe bytes 0x31,0x36,0x37,0x39(
ASCII values) .NOTE ASCII value for1is31and for9is39.
•Both text fileand binary filekeep record ofthe length ofthe file,and
identify theend offilewhen this isreached
•Intext files ,there isone more way todetect theend offile.The character
with ASCII value 26isconsidered tobeend offilecharacter intext files .All
input functions stop reading characters when this character isencountered
and return end offilesignal totheprogram
•Cdoes not insert this character infile ,itcan beentered through the
keyboard byCtrl +Z(Ctrl +Donsome systems) .Inbinary files nosuch
character represent end offile.
4
Difference between text files and binary files contd..
•Intext files newline isstored asacombination ofcarriage return ‘\r’
(ASCII 13)and linefeed ‘\n’(ASCII 10)while inbinary files newline is
stored only as‘\n’(ASCII 10).
•Inbinary format ,the data isstored inthe same way asitis
represented inmemory sonoconversions have totake place while
transferring ofdata between memory and file
•Intext format some conversions have totake place while transferring
ofdata between memory and file.
-For example while writing toatext file newline (‘\n’)has tobe
converted tocombination of(‘\r’)and (‘\n’)and while reading from text
filethis combination (‘\r’)and (‘\n’)istobeconverted back (‘\n’).
5
Difference between textfiles andbinary files contd ..
•The input and output operations in the binary files take less time as 
compared to the text files because no conversion has to be taken place 
•However the data written using binary file system is not very portable 
because size of data type and byte order may be different on different 
machines 
•In text format , these problems do not raise so it is considered more 
portable
•If the amount of numeric data stored in a disk is large, text mode is 
inefficient as numbers are stored as strings and hence more memory is 
required
6
File opening modes
•There are three file opening modes
•r  Opens the file for reading only
•w Opens the file for writing only
•a Opens the file for appending (or adding) data to it
•If the purpose is reading , and if the file exists, then it is opened with 
the current contents; otherwise an error occurs
•When the opening mode is writing , a file with the specified name is 
created, if the file does not exist; the contents are deleted when the 
file already exists
•When the purpose is appending , the file is opened with the current 
contents; a file with the specified name is created, if the file does not 
exist
7
File opening modes contd..
•r+ the existing file is opened from the beginning for both reading and 
writing
•w+ Same as wexcept  both for reading and writing
•a+ Same as aexcept both for reading and writing
8
Basic File Operations
•There are 4 basic operations that can be performed on any file in C 
programming language. They are,
•Opening/Creating a file
•Closing a file
•Reading a file
•Writing in a file
Opening / creating a file
•FILE * fp;
•fp=fopen (“filename”, ”mode”);
•A file with name filename is opened and assigns an identifier to fp
•This pointer fpcontains all the information about the file and is used as link 
between the system and the program
9
Opening/Creating a file
•fp–file pointer to the data type “FILE”.
•filename –the actual file name with full path of the file.
•mode –refers to the operation that will be performed on the file. 
Example: r, w, a, r+, w+ and a+. 
•fclose () –To close a file
•Declaration: int fclose (FILE * fp);
•fclose () function closes the file that is being pointed by file pointer fp. In a 
C program, we close a file as below.
•fclose (fp);
•All files are closed automatically when the program terminates
•Closing a file explicitly is a good programming practice
10
EXAMPLE PROGRAM FOR FILE OPEN, FILE WRITE AND FILE CLOSE
•/ * Open, write and close a file : */
•# include < stdio.h >
•# include < string.h >
•
•int main( )
•{
• FILE * fp;
• char data[50];
• /* opening file*/
• printf ( "Opening the file test.c in write mode" ) ;
• fp= fopen ("test.c ", "w") ;
• if ( fp== NULL )
• {
• printf ( "Could not open file test.c " ) ;
• return 1;
• } 11
EXAMPLE PROGRAM FOR FILE OPEN, FILE WRITE AND FILE CLOSE 
contd..
•// printf ( "\n Enter some text from keyboard” \
• //           “ to write in the file testfile \n" ) ;
• printf ( "\n Enter some text from keyboard to write in the file testfile \n" ) ;
•/* getting input from user*/
•/* accepts a line and stores in data*/
• while ( strlen ( gets( data ) ) > 0 )
• {
• /* writing in the file*/
• fputs (data, fp) ;   
• fputs ("\n", fp) ;
• }
• // closing the file
• printf ("Closing the file test.c ") ;
• fclose (fp) ;
• return 0; 
•}
•OUTPUT:
•Opening the file test.c in write mode
•Enter some text from keyboard to write in the file test.c
